tables.title: Terrain model against the LOLA team's published average-sunlight maps (real data)
tables.note: 200 seeded random points per map. Published: share of time any part of the solar disc is visible from the surface (PDS LOLA GDR maps AVGVISIB_85S_060M_201608 and AVGVISIB_75S_120M_201608, LOLA team, method of Mazarico et al. 2011), read at the nearest map pixel. Computed: the same quantity from this app's ray-cast skyline, observer at 0 m, one 18.6-year cycle from 2016-08-01 in 3-hour steps. Differences are in percentage points. 'DEM used here' is the grid under the point (80 m: PGDA LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ; 240 m: PDS LDEM_75S_240M; 474 m: SVS ldem_64; 1.9 km: PDS LDEM_16), with coarser grids beyond its edge. The published maps were computed on the LOLA team's own 60 m and 120 m grids, so part of the difference is the DEM, not the method.

tables.title: Published ridge-top results at the stated coordinates and heights (real data, 80 m DEM here against 20 m DEMs there)
tables.note: Each cell: average illumination % / solar visibility % (any part of the disc) / longest shadow. Computed with the 80 m LOLA mosaic from 2017-01-01 for 20 years in 1-hour steps, the period of Glaser et al. 2018. The published figures are each paper's best pixel on a 20 m DEM; an 80 m grid cannot place an observer on a crest a few tens of metres wide, so single points differ by several points either way. 'Best nearby' is the best-lit point on a 5 x 5 neighbourhood of 80 m steps around the published coordinates. Published values were read through a web-fetch tool (not byte-exact). Read the C1 rows with the two tables that follow: the 2 m match sits at the top of the range found within 100 m of the point, and the 0 m rows rest on the near-field sampling convention.

tables.title: Earth visibility: the one published per-site table found (Bryant 2009) could not be co-located, so it tests nothing
tables.note: Shown so the gap is visible. Each cell: share of time with at least 0 % / 50 % / 100 % of the disc above the skyline, observer 2 m above ground. Published: Bryant 2009, JPL IPN PR 42-176, Goldstone radar DEM at 40 m, 2009-2028, daily steps. Computed here: LOLA 80 m mosaic, one 18.6-year cycle in 3-hour steps. Bryant's sites are illumination maxima on a radar DEM in a different frame. At the stated coordinates the LOLA terrain is off the crest (Sun 14 to 40 % against a published 77 to 95 %), and the best-lit point within 1.2 km on the LOLA grid (160 m search steps, chosen on sunlight only) still does not reach the published sunlight, so these are not the same places and the Earth columns cannot be compared. The Earth side is checked against the LOLA team's own Earth-visibility maps instead, where they are installed: see the Earth tile above and its table below. Also tested: the skyline (against the sunlight maps above, in every direction) and the direction of the Earth (against JPL Horizons). Published values were read through a web-fetch tool (not byte-exact).
columns: Computed Earth at best-lit point nearby
Computed Sun at best-lit point nearby

tables.title: How the answer changes with DEM resolution: calendar year 2027, observer 2 m above ground
tables.note: Each site computed four times from real LOLA grids of different resolution, then on the smooth sphere. Hourly samples. 'Sunlit' uses the half-disc rule; darkness means no part of the Sun visible.

tables.title: Well-lit ridge pixels: where the average agreement does not hold (real data)
tables.note: The 60 m LOLA map rates 1612 pixels (0.0063 % of the map) above 60 % sunlit. A seeded sample of 60 of them (seed 20261115) was computed exactly as in the table above (0 m, any part of the disc, one 18.6-year cycle in 3-hour steps). Selecting on a high published value pulls the computed mean down by itself, so part of the negative mean difference is selection; the scatter is real. This row is the first random draw; the next table repeats it on other seeds.

tables.title: Well-lit ridge pixels on 10 seeds: a range, not one draw (real data)
tables.note: The ridge-pixel check repeated with other random draws of 60 pixels from the same 1612 pixels the 60 m Sun map rates above 60 %. Seeds: the seed of checks a and f (20261115) and the next 9 integers after it, a rule fixed before those runs were made. Sun columns: any part of the solar disc, against the 60 m Sun map. Earth columns: the same pixels against the 60 m Earth map, with the map's rule (any part of the disc) and with the mission card's rule (the Earth's centre). Differences are in percentage points, model minus map. A single pixel that is far off moves a 60-pixel mean and its correlation a good deal: read the Sun figure on ridges as this range.
columns: Earth's centre (the card's rule): mean difference

tables.title: How firm is the match at the connecting ridge (C1, 2 m)? Not very (real data)
tables.note: The same computation as the ridge-top table (2017-01-01, 20 years, hourly), repeated with the point moved, the observer raised or lowered, and the nearest ground sampled more finely. Each cell is the range over the variants. The agreement at the stated point is real but sits at the top of this range.

tables.title: Ground-level (0 m) crest values depend on how the nearest ground is sampled (real data)
tables.note: Average illumination at two published 0 m points against the distance of the first ray sample. The app uses one grid spacing (80 m), the node-to-node convention of the LOLA team's maps: a grid holds no information about nearer ground, and sampling the interpolated surface closer measures the interpolation. The agreement of the 0 m rows in the ridge-top table rests on that convention. The page offers 2 m and 10 m only.

tables.title: What sets the longest darkness at C1 (198 h here, 112 h published): ground a few hundred metres away
tables.note: During the longest computed dark run the Sun's upper limb stays just under a skyline set by nearby terrain, which an 80 m grid resolves poorly. Longest darkness on a ridge site is therefore indicative only.

tables.title: Earth visibility against the LOLA team's Earth maps (real data)
tables.note: Same 400 seeded points as the Sun check, observer at 0 m, one 18.6-year cycle in 3-hour steps. The map's own definition, from its label: This data product is a map of the average illumination by the Earth disc of the Lunar South Pole at a resolution of 60 m/pix by 60 m/pix, true at the pole in polar stereographic (spherical) projection. The calculations are based on the LOLA elevation map LDEM_85S_060M and are described in [MAZARICOETAL2011]. The values are continuous between 0 (permanent shadow) and 1, and indicate the percentage of timesteps where each pixel was sunlit (by any fraction of the Earth disc). Note a scaling was applied to fit the data in the INT16 value range. This label describes an IMG file in the form of a binary resampling with pixel registration. The label names no observer height and no time span; the maps are computed from the 60 m and 120 m LOLA grids, this build from the 80 m mosaic. Four rules are computed here so the definition can be seen to matter: only the row marked as the map's rule is the check. The mission card counts Earth contact by the Earth's centre, a stricter rule than the map's, so it reports fewer hours than this map would.

tables.title: The Earth check with and without the points that agree trivially, and the mission card's rule (real data)
tables.note: At some of the random points the map and the model are both exactly 0 (the Earth never rises there) or both exactly 1 (it never sets). Those points agree by construction and pull the mean difference down, so each map is listed twice: with every point, and without them. "Exactly" is to the four decimals stored for each point (under 0.005 % of the time). The any-part rule is the one the maps' labels state and the one the tile reports. The centre rule is what the mission card counts as Earth contact; it has no published reference of its own, and its rows show how far below the map it reads. Differences are in percentage points, model minus map.

headline.k: Sunlit share against the LOLA team's published map: ordinary terrain
headline.s: mean |difference| at 200 random points within 5° of the pole, correlation 0.9916; smooth sphere at the same points: ±33.2 pts. Rule: any part of the solar disc above the skyline, as the map's label states; the mission card's default asks for half the disc, which is stricter. Most of these points are poorly lit; see the next tile for ridges.

headline.k: The same check on well-lit ridge pixels, where landers would go
headline.s: mean |difference| at 60 seeded pixels the 60 m map rates above 60 %: the range over 10 random draws (median 4.3), correlation 0.41 to 0.75. First draw (seed 20261115): ±4.0, mean difference -2.8, 68 % within 5 points. Rule: any part of the solar disc above the skyline. An 80 m grid cannot hold a crest a few tens of metres wide.

headline.k: Earth in view against the LOLA team's Earth-visibility map
headline.s: mean |difference| at 200 of the same random points within 5° of the pole (±0.97 pts to two decimals), correlation 0.9946. Without the 53 points where the map and the model are both exactly zero (the Earth never rises there): ±1.31 pts at 147 points, correlation 0.9898. Rule: any part of the Earth's disc above the skyline, the rule the map's own label states. The mission card does not use this rule: it counts the Earth's centre, which is stricter and reads 3.5 points lower than this map at the same points (4.8 without those 53). 120 m map: ±0.69 pts, correlation 0.9984 (±1.11 pts, correlation 0.9957 without 76 points where the map and the model are both exactly 0 or both exactly 1); on 60 well-lit ridge pixels: ±1.57 pts, mean difference -0.2, correlation 0.9707 (±1.30 to ±1.98 pts on 9 other random draws).

headline.k: Shackleton connecting ridge, 2 m above ground: time with any Sun
headline.s: published 92.1% (Glaser et al. 2018, 20 m DEM). The match is not firm: within 100 m of the point the model gives 72.5 to 92.5%. Smooth sphere at the same point 55.6%. Rule: any part of the solar disc above the skyline.
